Newly hatched Eastern newts emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably small size, with a snout–vent length at birth of just 0.41 cm [Lb = 0.41 cm], a dimension derived from a total length estimate of 0.75 cm following standard morphometric conversions for the genus. These diminutive larvae, still bearing a residual yolk sac, must quickly transition to exogenous feeding once their mouthparts become functional. The duration of the aquatic larval stage is subject to considerable geographic variation, but metamorphosis typically occurs when the developing eft reaches a snout–vent length of roughly 2 cm , a threshold that marks the completion of gill resorption and the onset of a more terrestrial existence. After leaving the water, the juvenile eft embarks on a protracted growth phase that may last several years before reproductive competence is achieved.

Females of the Eastern newt eventually attain a maximum adult snout–vent length of 4.7 cm [Li = 4.7 cm], representing the upper limit of somatic growth observed in wild populations across their range. Males, in contrast, tend to reach a slightly larger ultimate body size, with an asymptotic snout–vent length of 5.1 cm [Li = 5.1 cm], a difference that likely reflects distinct selective pressures on male body size during aquatic courtship amplexus. This species exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is also mirrored in adult body mass. Using length–weight scaling relationships derived from the morphologically similar crested newt Triturus cristatus, the ultimate wet weight for females is estimated at 1.64 grams [Wwi = 1.64 grams], while the corresponding maximum mass for males reaches 2.1 grams [Wwi = 2.1 grams], a disparity that runs counter to the usual pattern of larger female mass in many amphibians.

Sexual maturation in female Eastern newts is initiated upon reaching a snout–vent length of approximately 3.6 cm [Lp = approximately 3.6 cm], a size that appears to signal the completion of sufficient fat storage and skeletal development for reproductive effort. However, some field studies have reported puberty occurring at a slightly smaller size of 3.4 cm [Lp = 3.4 cm], suggesting that local environmental conditions and resource availability can shift the timing of gonadal activation across different populations. Puberty itself is defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics, such as the enlarged cloaca and dorsal tail crest in males, though first reproduction may be delayed further as individuals accumulate the reserves necessary for successful courtship and egg deposition.

Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of its preferred lentic habitats, maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the Eastern newt sustains a maximum reproductive rate that reflects the species' modest annual output. Females typically deposit a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], each containing between 200 and 375 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 200 and 375 eggs per clutch], which are attached individually to submerged aquatic vegetation. This low-frequency, single-brood strategy is consistent with the life history of a long-lived iteroparous amphibian that invests in somatic persistence over high annual fecundity. The combination of a single annual clutch and a moderate clutch size means that the daily reproduction rate, integrated over the year, remains relatively modest, a pattern that is energetically sustainable given the species' reliance on seasonal prey pulses.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Notophthalmus viridescens under controlled conditions at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] reaches approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years], a remarkable longevity for a temperate-zone urodele that underscores a fundamentally slow-paced life history strategy. This extended lifespan allows individuals to buffer against years of poor reproductive success by breeding repeatedly across many seasons. The species' capacity for high survival through both its aquatic and terrestrial phases, coupled with its delayed maturation and relatively low fecundity, places it firmly at the slow end of the slow–fast continuum of amphibian life histories. Comparative data from other notophthalmine salamanders suggest that this extreme longevity may be linked to effective cryoprotectant mechanisms and low resting metabolic rates that minimize cumulative cellular damage over decades.
